When interleague first started in the 90s, the teams you played were almost random. The exception was your "natural rival," the team which in most cases was geographically closest to you (Yankees-Mets, Rays-Marlins, etc.). You played that team every year. When they expanded interleague in 2013, they gave it some structure: you played all the teams in a specific division, which rotated from year to year. However, they kept the "rival" concept by adding a two-and-two series that would be played each year no matter what other teams you played in interleague. The exception is when the interleague division you play is the same one in which your rival plays. In that case, your rival simply becomes part of your normal interleague schedule. The two-and-two series, however, remains in the schedule (somewhat inexplicably), and is played against *another* team in that division. That's what's happening this year: each division is playing its interleague counterpart (East vs. East, etc.). Since all the rivals are now lined up by division, the two-and-two series isn't played against the rival, but against another interleague team.

Many many years ago the broadcast affiliates would run syndicated shows when they weren't in network prime time. The morning and afternoon had soaps, some morning talk shows, and maybe a noon news, but the rest of it was syndication. One affiliate per market would get Wheel and Jeopardy, the other game shows were scattered about the grid, and then it was cartoons, sitcoms, and Westerns/dramas. This went through about 5-7pm when the affiliates would run their respective local news programs, the national news, and then prime time would start. That was followed by the late local news and the talk shows, if the network had one. Then it was back to syndication, which late at night devolved into infomercials and preachers. In the *really* old days some affiliates would shut off and run a test pattern. A new network became the fourth network in the late 80s, and though its grid increased steadily over time, it didn't really reach the same solid programming status as the Big Three until it took over sports coverage in the mid-late 90s. So it was sort of a mix between a "real" network and an independent UHF-style station. It had popular shows and so on but there was no talk show (sorry Chevy) and, in my market, no local news. That gave it a bunch of extra time for evening syndication. So there was a time in the mid-90s when the local affiliate aired three episodes of the show every weeknight. Every. Night. Three hours of the show. That's a season in less than two weeks. There was also a span in which it was two episodes of the show and an older series, but it was still three hours of the franchise *every night.* On *network TV.* Now, to the younger generation who grew up with on-demand binge-watching, three episodes a day probably doesn't sound all that insane. But DVDs, let alone streaming services, weren't even in our imaginations then. You could subscribe to a service where you got a 2-episode VHS every month or so, or you could tape the show when they aired the rerun. And that's what we did, all of us. Every fan over a certain age has, or had, a pile of videocassettes in their entertainment center. So this was how we watched the franchise. Indeed, this is how we *started* watching the franchise. Every night. Saturated by it. It's no wonder we were hooked. The next show ran on either our NBC or UPN affiliate, I forget which. Maybe it switched during the run. When it went into reruns, I think it was stuck down at around midnight. Not sure if the third show *ever* went into reruns here, and by the time the fourth show came along the idea of network affiliates filling up their off-hours with old shows seemed to have taken a backseat to judge shows, trashy talk shows, and reality, reality, reality. But that's what I remember: the show, always there on the local station. Watching the show instead of doing homework, watching the show instead of building social skills, watching the show and enjoying every minute. I don't know if I would have been a fan without those reruns. I certainly wouldn't have been so obsessed with the franchise without them. I suppose having them all on Netflix is better for everyone. The comics aren't canon. Just because a work is referenced doesn't make the work an official part of continuity. As an example, a character's first name originally appeared in a promotional novel in 1982. It wasn't given on screen until 2009. Does that make the promo novel canon? It doesn't. It makes the novel's use of the name canonically correct. I believe the reboot crew has made statements along the lines of "the tie-in comics are canon," but they don't have the authority to make that literally true. They are free to consider those comics as a part of the story they're telling, but nothing in them is part of official continuity unless and until it has been presented on screen.

It's not splitting hairs; that's how canon is defined. By the studio, by the network, and by us. Canon is stuff on screen. There are some very good reasons to keep it that way: it's easier to maintain creative control when you're only worrying about one level of media, it's easier for producers and writers to adhere to it, and the other levels of media (such as print) aren't nearly as accessible to the public. We - the studios and the fans - have all made a general agreement to respect that line (at least with regard to *official* canon...each of us is free to maintain their own "head canon"). When new producers or writers are brought in to make a new film or series, they are essentially given permission - by the studios and fans - to make new canon. When a fan rants about how much they hate the new films, part of the reason is because they "must" accept those films as having equal standing to the rest of the canon franchise (again, individuals can decide what personal canon is for them...we're talking about *official* canon). The producers have *not* been given permission - by us or by the studio - to alter the *definition* of canon.  Again, the reboot crew can draw from whatever sources they wish when making their films. I'm sure that in the writers' room there are giant whiteboards filled with background information about the world they're playing in, stacks of notes and charts and all sorts of things. If they want to publish some of that in comic form, no one is stopping them, certainly not the studio marketing department. I've read some of those comics and they're very good. I even incorporate stuff like "Countdown" into my own head canon. These comics are effectively *their* head canon. But they're not within the boundaries of what we've collectively decided is official. A producer can't change those boundaries just by saying so.

I've speculated on evolution in the sci-fi world before and it is a subject that I enjoy discussing. A specific episode explicitly states that humans (and all other humanoids) are a product of intelligent design. We find no evidence of this today, because we don't have the technology to examine our DNA in such detail and because we don't have other trees of life to compare it against. The modern theory of natural selection is either *wrong* or *subdued* by the seeders' actions (i.e. the seeders themselves may have evolved through natural selection). The question is: how did everyone explain the abundance of humanoids *before* that episode? What did Federation biologists say when people asked them why all aliens looked similar? The original series mentioned something called "Hodgkin's Law of Parallel Planet Development," but if we are to take it at its name, then it's a *law*, which defines physical properties and interactions, and not a *theory*, which explains *how* those laws work. So what was the *theory* of anthropomorphized exobiology? My feeling is that Federation scientists had already guessed at the existence of the seeders. In our world, when we make contact with actual aliens, we do not expect them to have any remote resemblance to us. It would be weird to find an alien with *blood*, or even a stomach or brain, let alone a humanoid. But as the Vulcans and other species gradually made first contact with one another, they would have been astonished to find not just humanoids, but *mammals*...and species who can successfully reproduce with one another. We can't impregnate a chimp, but Spock, Troi, Torres, and countless other examples show that aliens can intermingle. That should be *impossible* in naturalistic evolution, and so the prevailing ideas *must* have gravitated toward directed panspermia. Galen's work simply confirmed what they had already suspected. Incidentally, that episode indirectly forgives what are seemingly unscientific principles in another episode. That episode portrays crewmembers "de-evolving" into other forms of life, claiming that those forms of life are still vestigially present in "junk" DNA in extant organisms. But cats didn't evolve from iguanas, and humans didn't evolve from spiders. My theory is that the humanoid form was *not* the only thing the seeders wanted to preserve. They valued all the life on their planet, and wanted to make sure that all its legacy was passed on. So they encoded the patterns of tons of animals, not just humans, and the "program" went about its merry way, spitting out a lizard here, a rat there, and so on. This explains why many creatures on other planets are basically just weird variants of Earth creatures: O'Brien's tarantula, the needle snakes, viruses...even targs are just ugly pigs. And in order for each planet to eventually produce each animal, *every life form on every planet must contain the code for every animal provided by the seeders.* It's like the Ultimate Question being programmed into Arthur Dent's head. Barclay has the spider program in his DNA...and the fish program, and the fungus program, and so on. We all do. As far as natural selection, what might happen is that the program tries out different mutations every now and then, and if they happen to survive in the environment then they live on and the program goes a little further. This would mean that it's always trying every pattern, and thus you get examples of divergent evolution: in real life you have Old World and New World vultures, and in the series you have Humans and Voth.

Well, I'm talking about *teleportation* in the real world, which doesn't actually transfer matter. It just transfers information, which could theoretically be applied to matter states. Effectively a real-world teleporter is going to create a duplicate of the object...whether it destroys the original or not depends on the specific technology. We ought to agree that if you're duplicated and the original you remains, it is clearly a new person with a new consciousness even if no one (including the copy) can tell the difference. But if the original you is discarded, that's the only change in the teleportation process. It's still a copy of you at the other end. The copy would experience stepping into the machine and jumping to the other machine; the original would experience stepping into the machine and dying. To believe a real-world teleporter didn't kill you, you would have to demonstrate that consciousness can exist outside the body, and there's no actual evidence in favor of that...consciousness is simply an emergent property of the physical brain. Even if you could do that, you'd have to figure out how (and if) the consciousness can make the jump from your old body to your new one. How would it know where to go? The difference between teleporters and the Trek transporter is that the transporter takes the actual matter and beams it to the destination in the form of energy, where the matter is reassembled, not duplicated. We don't know of any way to actually do that in real life, but if we did then there would be a more substantial debate over whether you're still the same "person" on the other side. Incidentally, sleep is not actually a state of unconsciousness...it is an altered state of consciousness. There are forms of sleep which might serve your analogy, but from a certain point of view, it is possible for a person to live their entire lives without a strict break in their stream of consciousness, despite sleeping every night. With that in mind, it's less likely that you might "die" between the evening and morning, although the analogy might still hold for states of true unconsciousness. Nevertheless, it would apply only to the Trek-style transporter where matter is moved, not to the real-world style teleporter where matter is duplicated. In the real world, the necessity of death (or cloning) would be a topic for experts in the field, whereas in the Trek world, the possibility of death would be a topic for philosophers. I argue that it's not really that much of a possibility, because if it were, there would be far more people who would refuse to step into one and Starfleet would not use it on people without permission. Note that we know of only three characters who didn't like the transporter (Bones, Pulaski and Barclay), and their concerns involved accidental death...they never raised the question of consciousness transfer at all.

It was ultimately a poor decision. After the look of an alien species was changed we were unofficially expected to just accept that they "always" looked like that. It's a misconception that what we see or hear in canon is necessarily what is actually being seen or heard by the characters. One notable example is a trial scene in a later film. As the scene opens we hear the aliens speaking their language, and we are explicitly shown a clerk feeding the English translation into the characters' headsets. Once the language barrier is established, the scene abruptly shifts and the aliens are now all speaking English. Did they randomly switch? No, because at one point a character says "don't wait for the translation." The film employs a conceit: it sets up that two different languages are being spoken, but then uses only the language we understand because translations and subtitles (and inventing a fictional language) is too cumbersome for the gravity of the scene. The same conceit is employed in an episode where we hear aliens speaking perfect English but the humans hear their language. This shows that the alien doesn't speak English and never has; every time he has spoken in the series he is speaking a foreign language that is being converted to English, not just by the universal translator but by the show itself. This must happen in any scene in which aliens are speaking to each other with no humans around: the bridge of a rival ship, the war room, two characters bickering, and so on. The characters *can't* be speaking English, and so even though we hear English, we accept (as canon, no less) that they are speaking something else. So if that's true for language, there's no reason it can't be true for visuals as well. This *must* be the case every time they recast a character, like a female officer or a famous inventor or pretty much everyone in a reboot timeline. Unless these characters all got drastic cosmetic surgery, it's taken for granted that we are to accept that the character "always" looked like that. Note that the aliens in the original series didn't have bumpy eyebrows. The cyborgs got gnarlier post-the next generation. And that's to say nothing about what they did to the symbiotes and the reptilians. But nobody ever complains about those changes...it's just the aliens we nitpick. In the original series we meet a representation of a legendary figure. He is depicted as an original-series-style alien. Why? The augment virus was long after his time. When we meet his clone in the next generation, he is a latter-day alien. Which is the "true" appearance of the legendary figure? We also encounter original-series-style aliens like a famous captain and his friend, who later appear as "real" aliens in a later series. And of course all aliens in the early series up to season 4 were new-style. It was quite clear that up to season 4, the intent of the shows' creators was that the aliens always looked like the next-generation-era aliens, and that we should just pretend that the original series fit in. Most of us, even canon sticklers like me, were perfectly willing to accept that. When the later series did the "we don't discuss it with outsiders," they technically *did* canonically establish the difference, *but* it was meant as a cute joke, and they wisely left it open for interpretation (and endless argument). The issue should have been dropped there. Instead they wrote a story in which the difference is finally explained by the augment virus. It's a good story! But it hamstrings the franchise into honoring a visual conceit as a real, canon phenomenon. A recent series must now depict the aliens as original-series-style, which will look very strange indeed, or suffer from a blatant discontinuity which wouldn't have existed with just the later series joke. The reboot timeline depicted original-series-era aliens as next-generation-style, which is now anachronistic (obviously it's possible the virus was cured earlier in that timeline). I was perfectly fine with imagining the aliens as true aliens. I'm fine with imagining the original series ship as "actually" looking like a modern office (but I don't since I don't want to) and having technology appropriate to its relationship with the more modern early series and reboots. A normal analemma isn't especially complicated...you just take a picture of the sky at the same time and same place every day. I think most people use a tripod or something in their local area that they just never move. It's including the totality of a solar eclipse that takes a little bit more planning. Not just anyone can do an eclipse analemma, since eclipses only cover a small part of the earth's surface. And once you pick the spot, you have to know exactly when that spot will get totality, and that time of day is when you start the sequence (you could of course start it on the eclipse day just to be sure). As for the movements of the planets, that's the most fascinating part of astronomy to me, the clockwork of the cosmos, learning what *apparent* movement (what we see, like this analemma) has to do with *real* movement (what the system looks like from the outside). The usual example is seeing the outer planets slow down and reverse direction (over many months, measured by their position with respect to background stars)...this perplexed the entire species until we finally figured out it was because they were in superior orbits and we were "passing" them (Mercury and Venus do it too but for slightly different reasons and it's harder to notice). You'll often see people talk highly of ancient cultures like the Egyptians or Maya because they had "figured out" planetary movements, eclipse prediction, and so on. But they weren't any smarter, or had any more knowledge, than you or I. If you don't know anything about cosmic clockwork, it's because you spend your nights indoors watching TV. The cosmos was all they had. And once they figured out how to time agriculture to it, learning visual astronomy was critical to them. They knew Mars went retrograde and they knew when it would happen and for how long, but they didn't have any idea *why* it did. They didn't even know what Mars *was.* It was just a dot in the sky. They learned an extraordinary amount about the workings of the solar system with just their eyes and brains, but in the end it was all relatively obvious compared to what we've learned since the invention of the telescope and the development of the modern sciences.

It doesn't say it's the first professional game...it was the first game played in an official professional *league*, the National Association (which is considered by many sources to be a major league). The first all-professional *games* were played in the NABBP league, which wasn't necessarily a pro league but decided in the late 19th century to permit teams to openly pay players. The original club to go all-pro in that year was famously the first, and some of their opponents took the salary route too. Don't worry, the local historical site is still hallowed ground.

Well, there's not much I can say about the game other than by looking at the boxscore linked by someone else. But the boxscore doesn't give a complete view of what the game was like back then. The pitcher was obligated to throw what the batter wanted; the artistry came in pitching to contact rather than trickery (there were no breaking balls to speak of). In the early days of professional baseball, rules were quite different, such as fewer balls making a walk and the absence of a pitching mound. All four bases were square and set entirely within the corners of the infield (today, second base is offset, centered on the corner...not many people realize that). The home team could decide to bat first, and often only one ball was provided for the whole game. Many of these rules persisted well into a major league era, showing that even with a relatively sound organizational structure, baseball was still in the process of figuring itself out. A local team lasted only a season, playing a total of 19 games. Their opponent managed a record over two years. An early league was a loose, shifting amalgam of professional clubs (it is often not counted as a "major league"), but there were two franchises of note: a Boston team, an offshoot of the original Cincinnati ballclub that dominated the standings, and a Chicago team, who legitimately challenged the Reds although they had to sit out two years when their ballpark burned down in a major city fire. These two franchises made it into the current major league, and are still playing today as, respectively, an Atlanta team and a Chicago team.
